EHFD Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy  v.1                                                                                           Page 1 of 5 
East Hardwick Fire District #1 
 
Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy 
 
Adopted by the Prudential Committee on February 20, 2024 
 
 
Article 1. Authority. Under the authority granted in 24 V.S.A. § 2291(20), the Prudential Committee (Board 
of Trustees) of the East Hardwick Fire District #1 (EHFD), a state chartered municipality, hereby adopts the 
following policy concerning conflicts of interest and ethical conduct.  
 
Article 2. Purpose. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that the business of EHFD will be conducted in 
such a way that no public officer of the municipality will gain a personal or financial advantage from their 
work for the municipality and so that the public trust in its officers will be preserved. It is also the intent 
of this policy to ensure that all decisions made by public officers are based on the best interests of the 
EHFD. 
 
Article 3. Application. This policy applies to all individuals elected or statutorily appointed to perform 
executive, administrative, legislative, or quasi-judicial functions of EHFD.  
 
Article 4. Definitions. For the purposes of this policy, the following definitions shall apply: 
 
A. Conflict of interest 
A real or seeming incompatibility between a public officer's private interests and their public or 
fiduciary interests to the municipality they serve. A conflict of interest arises when there is a direct 
or indirect personal or financial interest of a public officer or a person or group closely tied with the 
officer including their spouse, household member, child, stepchild, parent, grandparent, grandchild, 
sibling, aunt or uncle, brother- or sister-in-law, business associate, or employer or employee in the 
outcome of an official act or action, or any other matter pending before the officer or before the 
public body in which the public officer holds office. 
 
A conflict of interest may take any of the following forms: 
 
1. A direct financial conflict of interest arises when a public officer acts on a matter that has a 
direct financial impact on that officer. 
2. An indirect financial conflict of interest arises when a public officer acts on a matter that has 
a financial impact on a person or group closely tied to the officer. 
 
 
 

 
EHFD Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy  v.1                                                                                           Page 2 of 5 
3. A direct personal conflict of interest arises when a public officer acts on a matter that has a 
direct impact on the officer in a non-financial way but is of significant importance to the 
officer. 
4. An indirect personal conflict of interest arises when a public officer acts on a matter in which 
the officer's judgment may be affected because of a familial or personal relationship or 
membership in some organization and a desire to help that person or organization further its 
own interests. 
5. A situation where a public officer has publicly displayed a prejudgment of the merits of a 
particular quasi-judicial proceeding. This shall not apply to a member's particular political 
views or general opinion on a given issue. 
6. A situation where a public officer has not disclosed ex parte communication(s) related to a 
quasi-judicial proceeding that is before the body to which that officer belongs. 
 
A "conflict of interest" does not arise in the case of an official act or action in which the public officer 
has a personal or financial interest in the outcome, such as in the establishment of a tax rate, that is no 
greater than that of other persons generally affected by the decision. 
 
B. 
Emergency means an imminent threat or peril to the public health, safety, or welfare. 
 
C. Ex Parte Communication means direct or indirect communication between a member of a public 
body and any party, party's representative, party's counsel or any person interested in the 
outcome of a quasi-judicial proceeding, that occurs outside the proceeding and concerns the 
substance or merits of the proceeding. 
 
D. Official act or action means any legislative, administrative, or quasi-judicial act performed by any 
public officer while acting on behalf of the municipality. This term does not apply to ministerial acts 
or actions wherein no discretionary judgment is exercised. 
 
E. Public body means any board, council, commission, or committee of the EHFD. 
 
F. Public interest means an interest of the municipality, conferred generally upon all residents of the 
municipality. 
 
G. Public officer means a person elected or statutorily appointed to perform executive, 
administrative, legislative, or quasi-judicial functions for the EHFD.  This term does not include 
municipal employees. 
H. Quasi-judicial proceeding means a case in which the legal rights of one or more persons who are 
granted party status are adjudicated, which is conducted in such a way that all parties have 
opportunities to present evidence and to cross-examine witnesses presented by other parties, and 
which results in a written decision, the result of which is appealable by a party to a higher authority. 
 
 

 
EHFD Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy  v.1                                                                                           Page 3 of 5 
Article 5. Prohibited Conduct. 
 
A. A public officer shall not participate in any official act or action if he or she has a conflict of interest, 
whether real or perceived, in the matter under consideration. 
 
B. A public officer shall not personally - or through any member of their household, business 
associate, employer or employee - represent, appear for, or negotiate in a private capacity on 
behalf of any person or organization that has an interest in an official act or action pending before 
the public body in which the public officer holds office. 
 
C. A public officer shall not accept gifts or other offerings for personal gain by virtue of their public 
office that are not available to the public in general. 
 
D. A public officer will not request or accept any reward, gift, or favor for taking an official act or 
action or advocating for or against an official act or action. 
 
E. A public officer shall not use resources unavailable to the general public - including but not limited 
to municipal staff time, equipment, supplies, or facilities - for private gain or personal purposes. 
 
F. A public officer who is a member of a public body shall not give the impression that he or she has 
the authority to make decisions or take actions on behalf of that body. 
 
Article 6. Disclosure. A public officer who, while serving on a public body, may have a conflict of interest, 
whether real or perceived, in a matter under consideration by that public body shall, prior to taking an 
official act or action or participating in any official act or action on the matter, disclose that he or she has 
an actual or perceived conflict of interest in the matter under consideration and disclose the nature of 
the actual or perceived conflict of interest.  Such disclosure shall be made as soon as practical upon the 
conflict or potential conflict becoming apparent to the public officer.  The disclosure may be made in 
writing to the other members of the public body, and consideration of the disclosure shall be addressed 
at the next meeting of the public body.  Disclosure may also be made during the course of a meeting of 
the public body.   
 
Alternatively, a public officer may request that another public officer recuse him or herself from a matter 
due to a conflict of interest, whether real or perceived.  (Such request shall not be considered an order 
for the officer to recuse him or herself.) 
 
Article 7. Consideration of Recusal. Once there has been a disclosure of an actual or perceived conflict of 
interest, other public officers shall be afforded an opportunity to ask questions or make comments about 
the situation. If a previously unknown conflict is discovered during a meeting or hearing conducted by a 
public body of the municipality, the public body shall take evidence pertaining to the conflict and, if 
appropriate, adjourn to an executive session to address the conflict. 
 

 
EHFD Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy  v.1                                                                                           Page 4 of 5 
 
Article 8. Recusal. 
 
A. Recusal of Appointed and Elected Officers. After taking the actions listed in Articles 6 and 7, a public 
officer, whether appointed or elected, shall declare whether he or she will recuse him or herself and 
explain the basis for that decision. If the public officer has an actual or perceived conflict of interest 
but believes that he or she is able to act fairly, objectively, and in the public interest, in spite of the 
conflict, he or she shall state why he or she believes that he or she is able to act in the matter fairly, 
objectively, and in the public interest.  Otherwise, the public officer shall recuse him or herself from 
the matter under consideration. A public officer that recuses him or herself may, but not must, 
explain the basis for that decision. 
 
B. Recusal of Appointed Officers. The failure of an appointed public officer to recuse himself or herself 
in spite of a conflict of interest, whether real or perceived, may be grounds for discipline or removal 
from office, as may be provided for in any of EHFD's by-laws, ordinances or regulations in effect at 
the time.  
 
Article 9. Recording. The minutes of the meeting or the written decision / minutes from the meeting / 
hearing shall document the actions taken in Articles 6 through 8. 
 
Article 10. Post-Recusal Procedure. 
 
A. A public officer who has recused himself or herself from participating in an official act or action by a 
public body shall not sit with the public body, deliberate with the public body, or participate in the 
discussions about that official act or action in any manner in their capacity as a public officer, though 
such member may still participate as a member of the public or private party, if applicable. 
 
B. The public body may adjourn the proceedings to a time, date, and place certain if, after a recusal, it 
may not be possible to take action through the concurrence of a majority of the total membership of 
the public body. The public body may then resume the proceeding with sufficient members present. 
 
Article 11. Enforcement. 
 
A. Enforcement Against Elected Officers; Consequences for Failure to Follow the Conflict of Interest 
Procedures. A public body shall review any and all suspected violations of this policy that may be 
brought before it, and make a determination if a violation occurred.  In cases in which an elected 
public officer has engaged in any of the prohibited conduct listed in Article 5, or has not followed 
the conflict of interest procedures in Articles 6 through 10, the EHFD Board of Trustees may, in its 
discretion, take any of the following disciplinary actions against such elected officer as it deems 
appropriate: 
 

 
EHFD Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct Policy  v.1                                                                                           Page 5 of 5 
1. 
The chair of the EHFD Board of Trustees may meet informally with the public officer to 
discuss the possible conflict of interest violation. This shall not take place in situations 
where the chair and the public officer together constitute a quorum of a public body. 
2. 
The EHFD Board of Trustees may meet to discuss the conduct of the public officer. 
Executive session may be used for such discussion in accordance with 1 V.S.A. § 
313(a)(4). The public officer may request that this meeting occur in public. If 
appropriate, the EHFD Board of Trustees may admonish the offending public officer in 
private.  
3. 
The EHFD Board of Trustees may admonish the offending public officer at an open 
meeting and reflect this action in the minutes of the meeting. The public officer shall be 
given the opportunity to respond to the admonishment. 
4. 
Upon majority vote in an open meeting, the EHFD Board of Trustees may request (but 
not order) that the offending public officer resign from their office. 
5. 
Referral of the violation to an agency for further ethical or legal review. 
6. 
Reconsider any decisions made pertaining to the matter for which there was a 
violation. 
 
B. Enforcement Against Appointed Officers. The EHFD Board of Trustees may choose to follow any of 
the steps articulated in Article 11A. In addition to or in lieu of any of those steps, the EHFD Board 
of Trustees may choose to remove an appointed officer from office, subject to state law and EHFD's 
by-laws in effect at the time.  It is noted that the by-laws at the time this policy is adopted state: 
"Any Prudential Committee member may be removed with or without cause at any time by the 
affirmative vote of a majority of the Members of the Fire District at a special meeting of the Fire 
District called for that purpose, and may be removed for cause by action of the Prudential 
Committee." 
 
Article 12. Exception. The recusal provisions of Article 8 shall not apply if the EHFD Board of Trustees 
determines that an emergency exists or that actions of a quasi-judicial public body otherwise could not 
take place. In such a case, a public officer who has reason to believe he or she has a conflict of interest 
shall only be required to disclose such conflict as provided in Article 6. 
 
Article 13. Effective Date. This policy shall become effective immediately upon its adoption by the EHFD 
Board of Trustees. 
 
 
UNANIMOUSLY ADOPTED BY ALL MEMBERS OF THE PRUDENTIAL COMMITTEE MEETING ON FEBRUARY 
20, 2024, AS RECORDED IN MINUTES OF THE MEETING.

documents.text:
EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 1 of 10 
 
East Hardwick Fire District #1 
Governing Ordinance 
 
Section 1: General 
1.1 Definitions 
Building:  
A structure that is authorized by the Town of Hardwick to serve as a residence or place 
of business, that is accessible by a public road, and that receives water service by way of 
a Service Line. For these purposes, a mobile home or camper is considered a Building. 
Consumer:  
The business or residential occupant of a Building that is connected to the District's 
Water System.  A Consumer may or may not be a Customer. 
Customer:  
The owner of the land upon which there is a building served by the District. Customer is 
responsible for maintaining the connection to the Water System, and paying all charges 
assessed by the District.  A Customer may or may not be a Consumer. 
Curb Stop: 
A buried valve installed along a Service Line that can be accessed using a riser at or near 
ground level. Curb Stops are owned and maintained by the District. 
Customer Side: That section of the Service Lines that is owned, by and required to be maintained by, the 
Customer.  The Customer Side begins as defined in Section 2, and ends where the pipe is 
first accessible within the Customer's structure. 
Distribution System: Any pipe or network of pipes that can deliver water to more than one Building or 
hydrant, regardless of where that pipe is located.  The District owns and shall maintain 
the Distribution System. 
District: 
The East Hardwick Fire District #1, acting through its Trustees 
District Side: 
That section of the Service Line that is owned and maintained by the District and begins 
where the Service Line connects to the Distribution System and ends where the 
Customer Side begins. 
Service Line:  
The section of pipe that connects only a single Building to the water Distribution System.   
Trustees: 
The Board of Trustees of the District, also referred to as the Prudential Committee.  
Water Rent:  
The annual fee which entitles the Customer to be connected to the Water System. 
Water System: The system of wells, springs, pipes, aqueducts, reservoirs, treatment and measurement 
equipment, service lines, and other infrastructure that provides water to Consumers of 
the District. 
 
 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 2 of 10 
 
1.2  Right of Entry and Inspection by District.  
The District shall have an ongoing unrestricted right of entry and access to each parcel and Building 
served by the District for all purposes necessary, advisable, or otherwise related to its ownership, 
operation, maintenance, repair and replacement responsibilities concerning the Water System. This 
right of access and entry shall include but not be limited to construction, installation, maintenance, and 
replacement of Water System components, periodic inspection and testing, and enforcement of these 
rules and regulations and collection of charges. The District shall exercise the right of access and entry in 
a good and careful manner and, unless emergency circumstances dictate otherwise, during reasonable 
hours and with notice to occupants and property owners.  When accessing buried Water System 
components, the District shall make a reasonable effort to protect existing plantings and landscaping to 
the extent practical, however such protection shall be limited to returning any dug or disturbed ground 
to the original grade and seeding with grass and/or mulching to prevent water erosion. 
1.3 Enforcement 
The District reserves the right to exercise all lawful means to enforce and maintain compliance with 
these regulations, including but not limited to assessing fines, filing liens, disconnecting a property from 
the Water System, pressing charges through a police agency, and litigation.  Any regulation herein may 
be waived for specific extenuating circumstances by a vote of the Trustees, such waiver to apply to all 
Customers and Consumers equally, and extenuating circumstances being limited to Acts of God or Force 
Majeure. 
Section 2: Service Lines and Curb Stops 
2.1  Start of Customer Side of Service Line 
The start of the Customer Side of the Service Line shall depend on the circumstances of the Service Line 
installation, as detailed below: 
A. If there is an existing Curb Stop located within five feet of the Customer's property line, on 
either the inside or outside of the property line, the Customer Side begins at that Curb Stop. 
 
B. If there is more than one Building on a parcel AND the point where the Service Line connects to 
the Distribution System is located on the Customer's property, the start of the Customer Side 
shall be a Curb Stop located after the point the Service Line connects to the Distribution System 
but before the Service Line enters into or under a Building, and that is fully accessible from 
outside the Building.  If more than one such valve exists, the Curb Stop shall be the valve closest 
to the point where the Service Line connects to the Distribution System, unless otherwise 
designated by the Trustees. 
 
C. If a Building or Buildings do not have a Curb Stop consistent with Section 2.1 A or 2.1.B,  the 
Customer Side starts at the point of the Service Line that is five feet on the inside of the 
Customer's property line, or at another point on the Service Line and within the Customer's 
property that might be specifically designated by the District for that particular property.  The 
District may install a Curb Stop on the point designated in this paragraph at its discretion. 
 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 3 of 10 
 
D. Any Building that does not have its own Service Line, but instead is served by a pipe from an 
adjacent lot, shall be deemed to have its own Service Line for the purpose of billing.  The 
Trustees may at their discretion require installation of a new, dedicated Service Line to the 
Building at any time.  For clarity, this paragraph is not meant to apply to a structure that 
receives water from a Building located on the same lot. 
 
2.2: Curb Stops and Temporary Shut-off 
 
A. Curb Stops and Service Lines shall not be removed, modified, or relocated by anyone aside from 
the District or with the Trustee's authorization.   
 
B. Except in emergency situations, no one may turn a Curb Stop on or off without prior 
authorization from the District.  If a Curb Stop is turned for an emergency reason without prior 
notification to the District, the District shall be immediately notified as soon as practical after 
the fact, even if the Curb Stop has already been returned to its prior position before notification 
is made.  No fee shall be assessed for turning a Curb Stop on or off if the reason for doing so was 
because of an emergency as determined by the Trustees. 
 
C. Except as allowed per Section 2.2(B), Curb Stops may be operated only by a designated agent of 
the District, or a licensed plumber.  If a Curb Stop is operated by an agent of the District at the 
request of a Customer, the District shall charge a service fee at the rate in effect at the time, as 
established by the Trustees. 
 
D. No credit or pro-ration of the Water Rent will be made in the event of a temporary shut-off.  If a 
Building does not have water turned on at the time an invoice for Water Rent goes out, the 
property will not be charged Water Rent.  However, if the water is turned back on before the 
end of the previously invoiced period, full Water Rent payment for the entire period will be 
required before the water is turned back on. Customers will be charged a service fee for turning 
a Curb Stop on or off, such fee to be set annually by the Trustees. 
 
The previous paragraph notwithstanding, in the case of a new owner of a property at which the 
water was off at the time they took ownership, or a property that had water shut off for more 
than one full year, or the initial turn-on of a new service installation, the District will turn the 
water on only after receiving both a) written or emailed request from the property owner of 
record for the water service to be turned on and b) payment of 25% of the annual water rent in 
effect for fiscal year during which the turn-on occurs.  After being turned-on, the Customer will 
be invoiced 25% of the annual water rent for each full quarter remaining in the fiscal year after 
the quarter during which the turn-on occurred.  This invoice will be due on the same schedule as 
water rent invoices for that Fiscal Year.  No additional fee will be charged for turning the water 
on in these cases. 
 
 
 
Section 3.0 Leaks, Waste, Conservation 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 4 of 10 
 
3.0 Use of Water 
Water drawn from the Water System shall be used in a manner customary and ordinary for domestic 
purposes or the business at a property when the property was first connected to the Water System, or 
subsequently authorized by the Trustees.   No Consumer shall install or use any plumbing or other 
apparatus which will affect the pressure or operating conditions of the Water System in a manner that 
would cause detriment, damage, or interference with the water service, as determined by the Trustees 
at their sole discretion.  All water drawn from the Water System is to only be used at the property where 
service is provided.  Transporting water drawn from the Water System to outside the District is strictly 
prohibited, except as may be directed by a Fire Department official.  Consumers shall use water only for 
customary and ordinary domestic purposes, or ordinary to their type of business.  In the event any 
Consumer should wish to utilize water for extraordinary demands, such as, but not limited to, servicing 
swimming pools or other unusual needs, or a new business or agricultural operation, the owner must 
obtain prior written approval from the District, with such conditions and extra payment obligations as 
the Fire District may determine. 
3.1 Leaks 
Customers are required to maintain the plumbing on their property in order to prevent and quickly 
repair any leaks and protect the plumbing from damage due to freezing.  Customers are responsible for 
repairing any leaks inside structures or on the Customer Side of Service Lines within 30 days of becoming 
aware of such a leak.  If the District suspects a leak on private property or on the Customer Side, the 
District may enter the property to confirm or locate any such leaks per Section 1.2.  If the District 
confirms a leak, it shall make a written demand to the Customer to repair the leak, within a reasonable 
timeframe determined by the District given the specific situation of the leak.  If the Customer does not 
fix the leak after three written demands, the Customer's service may be disconnected from the 
Distribution System consistent with Section 7.1. Each such written demand shall be not less than two 
weeks after the previous demand.  The District shall reconnect the  Customer to the Water System after 
it determines, at its sole discretion, that the leak was correctly repaired.  
3.2 Waste  
Discharging water for no practical purpose, or making water unfit for use, whether intentionally or 
because of negligence, is prohibited. 
3.3 Conservation 
The Trustees may declare a water conservation emergency at any time they deem necessary.  In 
declaring a water conservation emergency, the Trustees may stipulate conservation measures and 
limitations on usage, and penalties for non-compliance. 
Section 4. Billing and Non-payment 
4.1 Water Rent and Billing 
Charges for District services shall be assessed on a per Service Line / Building basis.  The Water Rent rate 
and frequency of billing/billing period shall be set at each annual meeting for the subsequent fiscal year.  
The Water Rent rate may be set taking into consideration the type and amount of usage in a Building, so 
long as the information used to set such rates is available in the public record.   

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 5 of 10 
 
4.1.1 Responsible Party 
The owner of record for each service address according to the Town of Hardwick Grand List used to 
prepare tax bills for the same fiscal year, herein referred to as the Customer, shall be invoiced and 
responsible for full payment of each year's full Water Rent.  The District will not issue pro-rated invoices 
or credits. 
4.2 Non-payment, late fees, and shutoffs for non-payment 
The following fees and collection actions shall apply whenever a Customer fails to make payment for 
Water Rent in full by the invoiced due date.  To ensure fairness to all Customers, these fees and actions 
will be applied uniformly in each case, without exception. 
A. As soon as practical after a payment due date has passed without payment in full, the District 
shall send a letter to the Customer notifying them of the balance due and requiring them to 
either immediately make payment in full, dispute the bill, or request a payment plan.  The letter 
will also inform the Customer that a late fee of 8% has been applied to the account, and that this 
late fee will be waived if full payment is received within 30 days of the original due date.  If full 
payment is not received in this time, the Trustees will not waive the 8% late fee under any 
circumstances, and 1%/month interest on the unpaid amount will also begin to accrue, starting 
with the original payment due date. 
B. If a Customer requests a payment plan prior to 30 days from the original due date, the Trustees 
shall waive the 8% late fee and interest payments.  The specific terms of the payment plan shall 
be at the sole discretion of the Trustees.  If a customer requests a payment plan after 30 days 
from the original due date, the Customer will no longer be assessed interest on the outstanding 
amount due but will be required to pay the penalty and interest accrued up to the point of 
requesting the payment plan.  A Customer who continues to make payments in accordance with 
an agreed-upon payment plan shall be exempted from the further actions required, below.  
However, should the Customer fail to make a payment in accordance with an agreed upon 
payment plan, the original penalty and interest payments shall be reinstated as of the original 
due date, except that the penalty and interest shall be applied to remaining outstanding balance 
due only.  Furthermore, should a Customer fail to make a payment plan payment without 
agreeing to a new payment plan, the required collection actions below will be reinstated. 
C. If full payment (including penalties and interest) is not received within 60 days of the original 
due date, a second notice shall be sent by certified mail to the Customer, and a copy of the 
notice shall also be affixed to the property door.   This notice shall inform the Customer that 
unless full payment, plus penalty fee plus interest, is received within 90 days of the original due 
date, a lien will be placed on the property.  This notice shall include a statement detailing the 
total amount due prior to the 90 days from the date of the original invoice due date.  
D. If full payment (including penalties and interest) is not received within 90 days of original due 
date, a lien for the amount due as of that date, plus a lien processing fee, shall be recorded in 
the Town of Hardwick land records.  A copy of the recorded lien shall be sent to the Customer, 
along with a letter describing what will be required to have the lien removed.   Even if a 
Customer agrees to a payment plan, and makes timely payment according to that plan, the lien 
shall not be removed from the property until full payment of all past due amounts, including 
penalties and interest, is made.  Furthermore, the Customer will be required to pay a lien 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 6 of 10 
 
release fee before the District removes the lien.  The notice shall also inform the Customer that 
the District may submit the lien to a tax sale process through the Town of Hardwick, and that 
such tax sale may be authorized at any time as determined by the Town of Hardwick.           
E. Following recording of said notice of lien, the lien may be foreclosed in the same manner as 
provided for foreclosure of real estate mortgages under Vermont law. Suit to recover a money 
judgment for any unpaid charge may be brought against the owner, and a foreclosure action 
may be brought to enforce the lien against the Customer's property. An action at law to obtain a 
money judgment against a Customer shall not be deemed to be an election preventing the Fire 
District from initiating a lien foreclosure action, nor shall any foreclosure action be deemed to 
be an election precluding the Fire District from maintaining an action at law for a money 
judgment against the Customer.  All costs including reasonable attorney fees incurred in making 
collection efforts, enforcing payment, and initiating and maintaining legal proceedings shall be 
added to and become part of the delinquent Customer's payment obligation. 
F. If full payment (including penalties and interest) is not received within 180 days of the original 
due date, the District shall move to shut off water service to the property per the following 
procedure: 
i. The District shall determine whether any resident of the property is protected 
from utility shutoffs for a medical reason, in accordance with 24 VSA § 5143.  If 
a resident of the property is protected from shut-offs, no further action shall be 
taken to shut-off service to the property.  So long as a past due amount remains, 
on the one year anniversary of the initial determination that a property is 
protected from shut-offs, the District shall confirm whether there continues to 
be a resident protected from shutoffs at the property, and if not, proceed with 
the shut-off procedure.  In addition, all collection actions required in this section 
will continue. 
ii. A notice printed on pink paper shall be affixed to the property door, and a copy 
sent by certified mail to the Customer.  The notice will inform residents of the 
date and location of a meeting of the Trustees at which they will vote to shut-off 
water to the property, the date of such meeting shall be least 30 days from the 
date the notice is posted at the property.   The notice will also inform residents 
of the property who are not the Customer to arrange a payment plan by which 
they would make payments on behalf of the Customer, to avoid shutoff of water 
service. 
iii. At the meeting of Trustees, referenced in the preceding paragraph, the Trustees 
shall review the account to confirm the history and circumstances,  that the 
Customer has not disputed the bill or sought a payment plan, or if entered into 
a payment plan failed to abide by it, and confirm that all steps and requirements 
for shutting off a utility customer as required by state law (including Title 24 
Vermont Statutes Annotated §5143 through § 5145) were followed.  If 
circumstances are found to be as expected, and all requirements for proceeding 
with a shut-off have been met, the Trustees will vote to proceed with the 
shutoff and fix a date for the shut-off.  Shutoffs shall not be scheduled to occur 
during the period between November 1 and March 31. 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 7 of 10 
 
iv. A notice shall be affixed to the property door and sent by certified mail to the 
Customer, warning of the Trustees' decision and the date of shutoff.  The notice 
will inform the Customer, and any residents of the property who are not the 
Customer, of actions needed on their part, to avoid shut-off. 
v. When service is disconnected to a Customer's property, the individual making 
the disconnection shall immediately inform an adult on the premises that 
service has been disconnected or if no responsible adult is present, shall leave 
on the premises in a conspicuous and secure place notification advising that 
service has been disconnected and the actions that the Customer or other 
occupant of the premises must take to have service restored.  The Town of 
Hardwick Health Officer shall be notified of any shut-off. 
vi. After shutting off service to the property, a fee for service shut-off because of 
non-payment will be applied to the account.  The fee for routine curb stop 
turning will be applied if the water service is later restored because of payment 
in full, or per a payment plan agreed to by the Customer. 
vii. Service that has been disconnected shall be restored  when the Trustees 
confirm the cause for disconnecting service has been remedied or when an 
agreement has been reached between the Customer and the District that 
provides, 
viii. to the full reasonable satisfaction of the District, for cure of the violation giving 
rise to the disconnection.  All costs of disconnecting and restoration of service, 
as well as fees or penalties required in these Rules, shall be borne by the 
Customer and shall be paid prior to re-connection.  
4.3 Disputed Bills 
1) If a Customer disputes a bill prior to the payment due date, and the District determines 
administratively that an error was made in calculating the bill, a new bill shall be issued and the 
erroneous bill voided without any penalty or collection action taken regarding the erroneous 
bill.  
2) If a Customer disputes a bill after the due date, the Customer will be required to make full 
payment of the bill before the District will consider the dispute.   If the District determines 
administratively that the bill was in error, it shall issue a corrected bill.  Any overpayment to the 
District shall be refunded within 30 days of the District issuing the corrected bill, and any 
underpayment shall be due within 30 days of the District issuing the corrected bill.  The 
penalties and collection actions required per Section 4.2 shall be applied to any underpayment 
not made within 30 days of the issuance of the corrected bill. 
3)   If the Customer continues to dispute the bill after the District found administratively that the bill 
was correct, or disputes a corrected bill, full payment of the disputed bill per the preceding 
paragraphs will be required before the District will further consider the dispute.  Once full 
payment of the disputed bill is made, they may request a hearing before the Trustees shall be 
held to consider the customer's dispute.  If the Trustees determine that the disputed bill or 
administratively corrected bill was in error, the District shall issue a corrected bill as directed by 
the Trustees.  Any overpayment to the District shall be refunded to the customer within 30 days 
of the District issuing the corrected bill, and any underpayment shall be due from the customer 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 8 of 10 
 
within 30 days of the District issuing the corrected bill.  The penalties and collection actions 
required per Section 4.2 shall be applied to any underpayment not made within 30 days of the 
issuance of the corrected bill. 
Section 5.0 Private Wells and New Service 
5.1 Private Wells 
No private well shall be established within the District service territory unless such a well is authorized in 
writing by the District. 
 
5.2 New Service and changes to lots or subdivisions, and changes of use 
No party may tap into, modify, or otherwise access water from the Water System without first receiving 
written authorization from the Trustees.  Prior to start of construction of a new Building, installation of a 
mobile home or camper pad, or changes to a lot (such as subdivisions or boundary adjustments), 
property owners must receive written approval from the Trustees for provision of water service to the 
new Building, potential future new Buildings, or modifications of infrastructure serving an existing 
Building.  As a condition of such approval, the Trustees may require the property owner to: a) provide 
engineering drawings of water service infrastructure to be built, b) record any such plans the District 
may require in the Town's land records prior to the sale of a property c) reimburse the District's costs for 
engineering review of the plans and an engineer's inspection of the construction of the new 
infrastructure, d) contract and pay for the construction of any new infrastructure the District may 
require, e) pay a service fee, at a rate established by the Trustees, for the District's review and 
management of the new service application, f) provide an escrow account, bond, or other security to 
ensure compliance with the plan and directions of the District or to compensate for damage to the 
Water System caused during construction of new infrastructure, g) require that the contractors installing 
new infrastructure provide written notice to any Consumers whose service might be impacted during 
the installation process, such notice shall be by door hangers unless otherwise approved by a Trustee, 
and such notice shall be given at least 48 hours before the period of expected impact, h) require that the 
period during which other Consumers might be impacted shall be no more than 4 hours, between 9AM 
and 4PM on weekdays, unless otherwise agreed by the board, i) other stipulations the Trustees may 
require to ensure a well-designed new infrastructure, that is correctly installed on, and the installation 
of which does not incur any costs to, or administrative burdens on the District.   
Any property owner applying to the Town of Hardwick to subdivide a lot or for a change of use shall also 
seek approval for the subdivision from the District.  The Trustees shall approve subdivision requests 
upon written acknowledgement from the current owner that any water service to the property will have 
to be through the District, and that the installation of any new service will be at the expense of the 
property owner.  This acknowledgement shall be recorded in the Town's Land Records upon acceptance 
by the Trustees.  The District shall require a subdivision application fee, which shall at a minimum cover 
the cost of recording the new service expense acknowledgement.  
 
After a new service has been installed, the District will turn on water service per Section 2.2 (D) of these 
Ordinances." 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 9 of 10 
 
5.3 Insurance 
Any contractor providing services under Section 5 shall provide a Certificate of Insurance naming the 
District as Additional Insured via a liability policy with minimum limits of one million dollars, and, if 
required by the State of Vermont, statutory Workers' Compensation insurance.  
6.0 Limits on Liability 
The District shall not have or incur any liability for quantity or quality deficiencies of water provided 
through the Water System to Consumers or Customers. 
7.0 Water Shutoffs and Disruptions 
7.1 Shutoffs 
The Trustees may at any time vote to shut off water to a Customer for any of the following reasons: 
1) Failure or refusal to pay for Water Rent or other charges, as described in Section 4.2. 
2) Waste of water through leakage or other exfiltration due to faulty plumbing or components on 
the Customer's side of the Curb Stop, and failure or refusal of the Customer to correct the 
deficiency causing the leakage or exfiltration. 
3) Failure or refusal by Customer to fulfill Customer's responsibilities to keep and maintain water 
pipes, plumbing, and fixtures within a Building in good order and repair and protected from 
freezing or other damage.  
4) Customer's or Consumer's willful damage to the water systems, obstruction of the water supply, 
or unauthorized tapping into or tempering with any portion of the Water System. 
5) Violation of any of the rules and regulations set herein by either a Customer or Consumer. 
6) In the event of fire or other emergency, as necessary to prevent injury, death, or loss of 
property. 
Shutoffs in the case of emergencies, per 7.1(6), may happen immediately and with no notice.  The 
process for shutting off service for any other reason shall follow the procedure described in Section 4.2 
(F) to the extent appropriate, depending on the reason for the shut-off.  
7.2 Disruption of Service 
The District may temporarily disrupt water service for purposes of maintaining, repairing, replacing, and 
upgrading the Water System. In such event, the District shall make all reasonable and practicable 
measures to notify or otherwise inform the Consumers of the temporary disruption. In the event of a 
water line break, emergency, or other unavoidable circumstances requiring immediate corrective action, 
the District shall not be required to provide any advance notice or warning to the Consumers. The 
District shall not be liable for any damage or claim for inconvenience or other event resulting from the 
temporary disruption. 
8.0 Miscellaneous Provisions  
8.1 Modifications and Amendments.  
The District through the Trustees may amend, modify, or waive any of the provisions contained herein 
subject to the requirements of all laws and regulations of the State of Vermont applicable to the Fire 

EHFD Governing Ordinance v1.1                             Approved July 21, 2026                            Page 10 of 10 
 
District and under such terms and conditions as the Trustees shall determine to be necessary or 
advisable in the interests of the Fire District. 
8.2 Word Meanings.  
Words such as "herein", "hereinbefore", and "hereof" refer to those Rules, Regulations, and Schedule of 
Rates and Charges as a whole and not merely to any particular Section in which the words appear. The 
singular shall include the plural, and the masculine gender shall include the feminine and neuter (i.e., 
his, her, them, they, etc.). 
8.3 Validity.  
Invalidation of any one or more of the rules, regulations, or provisions contained herein by a court or 
other tribunal as appropriate jurisdiction shall not affect in any manner the other rules, regulations, and 
provisions herein, which shall remain in full force and effect. 
8.4 Actions by District.  
All actions, authorization, rights, and powers of the District as provided herein may be exercised by the 
Trustees of the District, as the same shall be composed from time to time. The officers, employees, 
agents, contractors, and other authorized persons of the District shall conform under the direction and 
supervision of the Trustees and on behalf of the District.

documents.text:
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 1 of 7 
East Hardwick Fire District #1 
 
Procurement Policy 
 
Adopted by the Prudential Committee on February 20, 2024 
 
 
PURPOSE.  The purpose of this Purchasing Policy is to obtain the highest quality goods and 
services for the East Hardwick Fire District #1 (EHFD, or "the municipality") at the lowest possible 
price, to exercise financial control over the purchasing process, to clearly define authority for the 
purchasing function, to allow fair and equal opportunity among qualified suppliers, and to provide 
for increased public confidence in the procedures followed in public purchasing. 
 
AFFIRMATIVE ACTION. To the extent reasonably practical, qualified small, minority and women-
owned businesses shall be included in the solicitation lists for bids or non-bid purchases. If the 
purchase is federally funded in whole or in part, minority and women owned businesses must be 
included in the solicitation lists and all other affirmative action requirements outlined in the grant 
provisions must be followed.  
 
 
CODE OF CONDUCT. Employees, officers (including Trustees), and agents of the municipality 
involved in the procurement and selection of bids and purchases are required to abide by the 
EHFD's Conflict of Interest(COI) Policy at all times.  For the avoidance of doubt, EHFD's COI policy 
generally requires that no employee, officer or agent of the municipality shall participate in 
selection, award, or administration of a contract if a conflict of interest, whether real, apparent or 
potential, would be involved.  The COI policy further requires that an employee, officer or agent of 
the municipality who is involved in the procurement and selection of a bid or purchase and who 
has a real or apparent conflict of interest must disclose that conflict of interest, and such 
disclosure must be documented in the minutes for that meeting which shall be retained as part of 
the official record surrounding the bid or purchase.  The COI policy is the definitive and detailed 
policy regarding conflict of interest, and the foregoing statements are intended as a general 
summary only. 
 
Officers, employees and agents of the municipality will not solicit nor accept gratuities, favors or 
anything of monetary value from contractors, potential contractors, or parties to sub -agreements.   
 
Officers, employees and agents who fail to follow the above Code of Conduct shall be sanctioned 
or disciplined, to the extent permitted by law, for violations of the above standards.  
 
DOCUMENTATION. Records documenting the procurement process for any Minor or Major 
purchases, as those terms are defined below, including the reason for the specific procurement 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 2 of 7 
method chosen, the basis for the award and contract pricing (showing evidence that the process 
was fair and equitable), as well as any other significant decisions that were part of the 
procurement process shall be maintained for a period of at least three years from the date of the 
submission to the Federal government of the final expenditure report if the purchase or project 
was funded with federal grants, or until the completion of any litigation, claim, negotiation, audit, 
or other action involving the records, whichever is longer. Otherwise, records shall be maintained 
by the municipality in accordance with the retention and disposition schedules as set by the 
Vermont State Archivist.  Recurring purchases made under an agreement resulting from one bid or 
solicitation process may be documented, per this section, by reference to the first purchase or 
blanket agreement; documentation is not required for each recuring purchase if the purchase is 
made under a bid or solicitation that was previously documented. 
 
PURCHASING AUTHORITY 
 
Purchasing Agents. The following employees, agents, or officers are designated to act as 
Purchasing Agents for the municipality:  
 
1. Chairperson of the Prudential Committee (Board of Trustees) 
2. Any other Trustee who is not the Treasurer, and who is authorized by a vote of the Board 
of Trustees to be a Purchasing Agent 
3. An agent, contractor, or employee of the EHFD who is authorized by a vote of the Board of 
Trustees to make specific purchases 
 
Purchasing Agents are responsible for ensuring that the best possible price and quality are 
obtained with each purchase and Purchasing Agents shall review all proposed procurements to 
avoid unnecessary or duplicative purchases of equipment, supplies and services. Purchasing 
Agents shall also ensure that competition is not restricted with limits on the geographic location of 
vendors, with unreasonable requirements or qualifications placed on vendors, or by allowing 
vendors to be selected who have engaged in noncompetitive pricing practices.  
 
Incidental Purchases. Trustees who have been designated to act as Purchasing Agents may make 
purchases of up to $500 without prior approval, provided those purchases are limited to the 
amount of the budget authorized by the municipality.  Purchasing Agents who are not also 
Trustees shall not make Incidental Purchases. 
 
Minor Purchases. Minor purchases are those under $1000 and not an Incidental Purchase.  
Trustees who have been designated to act as Purchasing Agents may make Minor Purchases 
provided that they receive written confirmation from the Treasurer that the purchase is within a 
budgeted allocation, or is authorized by a vote of the Board of Trustees.  Purchasing Agents who 
are not also Trustees may make Minor Purchases only if specifically directed by the Treasurer or a 
vote of the Board of Trustees.  The previous restrictions notwithstanding, Purchasing Agents may 
also make Minor Purchases in the event of unplanned service outage that requires the immediate 
procurement of material or service in order to restore service.  Any such emergency procurement 
shall receive after-the-fact authorization by the Treasurer or Board within three business days of 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 3 of 7 
the procurement.  Although not required, competitive quotes from at least two vendors should be 
obtained whenever practical, especially for purchases over $100. Minor Purchases are not 
required to use a formal solicitation process. 
 
Major Purchases. All purchases over $1000 require prior approval of the Board of Trustees, and 
shall be undertaken in a manner prescribed by the Prudential Committee (Board of Trustees).  The 
Board of Trustees shall review all proposed procurements to avoid unnecessary or duplicative 
purchases of equipment, supplies and services.  The Board of Trustees shall also ensure that 
competition is not restricted with limits on the geographic location of vendors, with unreasonable 
requirements or qualifications placed on vendors or bidders, or by allowing vendors to be selected 
who have engaged in noncompetitive pricing practices. 
 
If federal funding is used for purchases between $10,000 ($2,000 in the case of construction 
projects subject to Davis Bacon requirements) and $250,000, price or rate quotes must be 
obtained from two or more qualified sources following the affirmative action provision of this 
policy and all provisions regarding fair and unrestricted competition. 
 
All quotes shall be solicited in a transparent and equitable basis, so that every potential bidder has 
the same information and equal opportunity to secure the purchase.  For all Major Purchases price 
and rate quotations shall be obtained from at least two qualified vendors to ensure that the 
municipality has received a fair and reasonable price. Vendors will be selected based on cost, the 
quality of the goods and services offered, and the ability, capacity, and skill of the vendor 
demonstrated under prior contracts with the municipality or as demonstrated through references, 
and any of the criteria indicated in Section 5, below, utilized in a Sealed Bid Process.   
 
FEDERAL FUNDING.  Projects or procurements of any value that are funded with federal dollars 
must follow a sealed bid process, either as outlined below or specified in grant requirements or 
federal regulations, and follow any procurement guidance as outlined in the grant agreement and 
applicable federal regulations.  In addition, a pricing analysis must be completed by the Purchasing 
Agent or a qualified consultant prior to issuing the request for proposals to ensure that there is a 
reasonable estimate against which to compare bid proposal pricing. 
 
SEALED BID PROCESS.  Purchases which are expected to exceed $250,000 must follow the sealed 
bid process specified here, or another sealed bid process adopted by the Board of Trustees for the 
particular solicitation.  The Board of Trustees may also direct that the sealed bid process be used 
for smaller value procurements. Procurements of any value that are funded with federal dollars 
must follow a sealed bid process consistent with grant requirements and federal regulations at the 
time of procurement.  Unless determined otherwise by the Board of Trustees for a particular 
solicitation, the sealed bid process shall consist of the following steps and requirements: 
 
1) Request for Bids. The sealed bid process shall be initiated by the issuance of a Request for 
Bids prepared by the Board of Trustees or its designee. Notice of the Request for Bids shall 
be made by letters to known providers soliciting bid responses, advertisements posted in 
at least three public locations within the municipality, and advertisements placed in a 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 4 of 7 
newspaper or on-line forums of general circulation in the region.  All potential bidders who 
respond to the notice of the Request for Bids shall be provided with the exact same 
directions for preparing and submitting bids, bid specifications, and be subject to the same 
deadlines. 
 
2) Bid Specifications. A list of bid specifications shall be prepared for each Request for Bids 
and shall be provided to each potential bidder responding to the Notice for Request for 
Bids, as well as any other party who may request it. Bid specifications shall include: 
 Bid name. 
 Bid submission deadline. 
 Date, location, and time of bid opening. 
 Specifications for the project or services including quantity, design, and 
performance features. 
 Bond and/or insurance requirements. 
 A copy of the proposed contract. 
 Any special requirements unique to the project or purchase. 
 Delivery or completion date. 
 For construction projects, language that sets a requirement for a bid guarantee in 
the amount of 5% of the bid price from all bidders, as well as performance and 
payment bonds in the amount of 100% of the contract price from the contractor 
awarded the bid. If federally grant funded, the bidders must also include costs for 
Davis Bacon compliance if that is a requirement of the federal agency providing 
the funding. 
 Means by which potential bidders may inspect the work site or ask questions 
regarding the Request for Bid.  Any such means shall be structured in such a way 
that all potential bidders will have access to the same information at the same 
time as all other potential bidders. 
 For federally funded construction projects over $2,000, a statement that 
contractors will be provided with a copy of the most current wage determination 
(from the DOL website at http://www.wdol.gov/dba.aspx) and must comply with 
the Davis Bacon Act. 
 Language that reserves for the Board of Trustees the right at its sole discretion to 
reject any and all bids, wholly or in part, to waive any informalities or any 
irregularities therein, to accept any bid even though it may not be the lowest bid, 
to call for rebids, to negotiate with any bidder, and to make an award which in its 
sole and absolute judgment will best serve the municipality's interest. Language 
that also reserves the right the Board of Trustees to investigate the financial 
condition of any bidder to determine his or her ability to assure service throughout 
the term of the contract. 
 
Once a Request for Bids has been issued, it shall not be changed without re-starting the 
bidding process unless the Request for Bids contains a provision for potential bidders to 
register by a date certain to receive updates and changes to the Request for Bid.  If a 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 5 of 7 
potential bidder registration system is used, all updates or changes will be exactly the same 
for each potential bidder, and provided to all registered bidders at the same time.   Parties 
other than potential bidders may also register to receive updates and changes. 
 
3) Bid Submission. All bids must be submitted in sealed envelopes, addressed to EHFD as 
specified in the Request for Bids, and plainly marked with the name of the bid and the time 
of the bid opening.  Bid proposals will be date-stamped on the outside of the envelope 
immediately upon receipt. Any bid may be withdrawn in writing prior to the scheduled 
time for the opening of bids. Any bids received after the time and date specified shall not 
be considered and shall be returned to the bidder unopened. 
 
Bidders shall bid to specifications and any exceptions must be noted by the bidder. A 
bidder submitting a bid thereby certifies that the bid is made in good faith without fraud, 
collusion, or connection of any kind with any other bidder for the same work, and that the 
bidder is competing solely on their behalf without connection with or obligation to any 
undisclosed person or firm. 
 
4) Bid Opening. Every bid received prior to the bid submission deadline will be publicly 
opened and read aloud by the Board of Trustees or its designated Purchasing Agent. The 
bid opening will include the name and address of bidder; for lump sum contracts, the lump 
sum base bid and the bid for each alternate; for unit price contracts, the unit price for each 
item and the total, if stated; and the nature and the amount of security furnished with the 
bid if required. 
 
5) Criteria For Bid Selection. In evaluating bids, the Board of Trustees will consider the 
following criteria: 
 Price. 
 Bidder's ability to perform within the specified time limits. 
 Bidder's experience and reputation, including past performance for the 
municipality. 
 Quality of the materials and services specified in the bid. 
 Bidder's ability to meet other terms and conditions, including insurance and bond 
requirements. 
 Bidder's financial responsibility. 
 Bidder's availability to provide future service, maintenance, and support. 
 Nature and size of bidder. 
 Contract provisions that are acceptable to the municipality. 
 Any other factors that the Board of Trustees determines are relevant and 
appropriate in connection with a given project or service. 
 
In addition to the above, in the case of a contract supported by federal funds, the 
additional criteria shall apply: 
 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 6 of 7 
 There shall be no preference exercised for local contractors or suppliers. 
 Minority and women-owned businesses must be included in the solicitation list 
for the request for proposal.  
 For construction projects over $2,000, contractor's indication of acceptance of 
wages in the current wage determination provided as part of the Request for 
Bids. 
 A bidder will not be accepted who is listed on the Excluded Parties List System 
website (https://www.sam.gov). 
 
6) Change Orders. Once a bid has been accepted, if changes to the specifications become 
necessary, the Board of Trustees will prepare a change order specifying the scope of the 
change. Once approved, the contractor and an authorized agent of the municipality must 
sign the change order. 
 
7) Exceptions. The following exceptions may apply, however there must be written 
documentation created and maintained that outlines the process and rationale for such 
exceptions: 
 
 Competitive Proposals. If time does not permit the use of sealed bids, or the 
award will be made on the basis of non-price related factors, a competitive 
proposal process shall be initiated by the issuance of a Request for Bids (RFB) or 
Request for Qualifications (RFQ) prepared by the Board of Trustees or its 
designee that includes the factors that will be used to evaluate and compare the 
proposals. Bids or qualifications shall be obtained from an adequate number of 
qualified sources (at least two vendors) to ensure that the municipality has 
received a fair and reasonable price and all notification and record keeping 
requirements of the sealed bid process shall be followed. If architectural or 
engineering services are being solicited, this process should be used with the 
most qualified firm or individual awarded the bid and price or fees negotiated 
after the award. If competitive proposals are used, all of the steps in the sealed 
bid process should be followed except that: 1) the bid submission need not be 
sealed; and 2) price will not be the primary factor in the proposal selection.  
 
 Sole Source Purchases. If the Board of Trustees determines that there is only 
one source for a proposed purchase, it may waive the bid process and authorize 
the purchase from the sole source.   
 
 Recurring Purchases. If the total value of a recurring purchase of a good or 
service is anticipated to exceed [$25,000] during any fiscal year, the bid process 
shall be utilized and shall specify the recurring nature of the purchase. Once a 
bid has been accepted, all future purchases shall be made from that bidder 
without necessity of additional bids, until such time as the Board of Trustees 
votes to initiate a new bid process. 

 
 
EHFD Procurement Policy                                                                                                                        Page 7 of 7 
 
 Emergency Purchases. The Board of Trustees may award contracts and make 
purchases for the purpose of meeting the public emergency without complying 
with the bid process. Emergency expenditures may include immediate repair or 
maintenance of municipality property, vehicles, or equipment if the delay in such 
repair or maintenance would endanger persons or property or result in 
substantial impairment of the delivery of important municipality services. 
 
 Professional Services. The bid process shall not apply to the selection of 
providers for services that are characterized by a high degree of professional 
judgment and discretion including legal, financial, auditing, risk management, 
and insurance services with a value of up to [$25,000]. 
 
 Non-competitive Purchases. Federally funded non-competitive purchases for 
$250,000 or more require a cost analysis to determine the reasonableness of the 
proposed pricing and should be completed in accordance with the requirements 
of the federal or state agency issuing the grant funding. 
 
 
UNANIMOUSLY ADOPTED BY ALL MEMBERS OF THE PRUDENTIAL COMMITTEE MEETING ON 
FEBRUARY 20, 2024, AS RECORDED IN MINUTES OF THE MEETING.

East Hardwick Fire District No. 1 Privacy Policy 
Adopted 7/21/2026 
 
What information do we collect from our customers and consumers?  We ask that customers 
and consumers provide an email address and/or phone number so that we can provide timely 
alerts regarding safety or service issues, disseminate information about our services and public 
processes as required by law, and reach individual customers to resolve billing issues.   
As provided under State law, we obtain the name and mailing address of owners of record of all 
properties within the District from the Town's Grand List. 
How do we collect this information?  We ask that customers and consumers voluntarily provide 
an email and/or phone number through notices on mailings, our website, and other routine 
communications.  Customers/consumers may provide this contact information through phone, 
email, mail, or conversation.  Providing this contact information is entirely voluntary.  We do not 
attempt to obtain contact information through third party sources. 
We obtain the name and mailing address of owners of record of properties within the District 
from the Town's Grand List, which is a public record. 
Why do we need this information and how do you use it?  Contact information of consumers 
and customers is used to disseminate notices regarding safety and water service conditions, and 
to provide notices as required by State or Federal regulation.  Examples include: To alert a "Boil 
Water" order, to notify of temporary water service suspension due to repairs, provide water 
quality test results, or to warn of District meetings.  We may also contact individual customers 
regarding issues specific to them, for example to conduct a leak detection survey on their 
property. 
The names and mailing addresses of property owners are used to assess water rent on the 
property, as provided through State law and the District's Charter and By-Laws. 
We do not share our customers' or consumers' information with anyone. 
How can customers/consumers opt out of email or text communications with the District? By 
texting/replying STOP, UNSUBSCRIBE, QUIT; or by requesting that communications be stopped 
to a Trustee through email or conversation.  If such requests are received, email or phone 
numbers will be removed from the District's records. 
How can customers/consumers request changes to their information? They can text or call the 
District's phone number, or email trustees@easthardwick.gov

Hardwick, like everywhere else, is on lockdown. The Board has 
decided that we will not open the Depot until July 1-- at the earli-
est.  Our most faithful volunteer, Lorraine Hussey, is 92 and indis-
pensable, so we factor her health into all the decisions we make. 
If you have a specific question, however, we will happily find the 
answer for you. Contact Lorraine at 802-472-5903 or Wiz at 802-
472-6424 or edow1@earthlink.net.
It may be just as well that we can't open. The construction of 
the Angell Room left a great mess throughout the building. While 
we have received about half the file drawers and shelving we need 
to set the Angell Room up for use, we have not even begun to put 
them in place because of the virus and the need for social dis-
tancing. Still on their shipping pallets, they fill what empty space 
existed in the old Freight Room after we crowded the contents 
from the Grain Store into it, so we could build the Angell Room in 
the first place. We had thought about holding a chicken barbeque 
and tag sale to get rid of the items we don't want, but we've had to 
cancel them. 
The Picture Project still dominates the Museum and the Meeting 
Room, though we see the end off in the distance. We have boxes 
of pictures for other towns on all the seats in the meeting room; 
Wolcott Street, Hardwick Vermont

3
filing the Hardwick pictures has taken over the Granite Room. The 
boxes we used for the Newspaper Project, which is now complete, 
take up all unused space in the Museum. In other words, the De-
pot is all confusion from end to end, and getting ready to receive 
company by the time you receive this issue of the Journal would 
take a Herculean effort - think Augean stables.
****
How researchers access materials marks one of the major differ-
ences between a library and a historical repository. In a library, the 
materials sit on a shelf that researchers can access themselves. 
Historical repositories contain materials that exist no place else, 
so, to protect them, repository personnel do all the retrieving. Re-
positories create inventories so researchers and volunteers know 
what we have and where we have it. The Picture Project Inventory 
now fills 46 pages of listings that describe the photographer's inter-
est. For example: we could categorize a picture of kids on a school 
playground by 1) the kids' names, 2) the game they are playing, 3) 
the location of the playground 4) the season of the year, etc. If the 
photographer wanted to highlight the new playground equipment 
at the school, we would file the picture in School pictures. If he or 
she wanted to feature kids enjoying themselves during summer 
vacation, we filed the picture under Recreation. If the children 
were models, showing off the latest fashions, we would file the 
picture under Fashion, but we don't have any of those.
Because we have such a large collection (roughly 15,000 im-
ages), we have divided it into large categories and subdivided some 
large categories into subcategories, so the researcher can browse 
effectively. Just seeing all Businesses listed together reveals a 
lot, and seeing them subdivided by type of business reveals even 
more. The category Businesses covers 4 pages of single-spaced 
listings, Families cover 4 pages, Individuals cover 11 pages, Or-
ganizations cover 4 pages, Schools cover 11 pages, Weddings 
and Engagements cover 3 pages, and we have 9 pages of other 
categories. We guide people through the inventory using notes 
to explain the difference between, for instance, Agriculture and 
Farms; we also use See and See Also references. We're not done 
yet, but we're well on our way.
Stay well.
The Publications Committee

More Bootlegging
Michael Michaud, (1950 - ), son of Laurier Alcide Michaud (1913-
2004) and Rose Mable [Keen] Michaud (1917-2001 ), sent us this 
recollection of bootlegging in East Hardwick during Prohibition. 
Today he lives in Red Lion, PA and Cambridge, MD. Now retired, 
he worked as teacher and insurance defense trial attorney. Many 
long years ago he was accepted to the graduate program at the 
Breadloaf School of English at Middlebury, but he never attended. 
Instead, he took an MA elsewhere, and, while in a doctoral program 
at Rutgers, he bolted for law school.  He wrote, "It's stories like my 
mother's herein that have always made me suspicious of govern-
ment, though if I had it to do all over again, I might've gone to work 
for our nations parks system".

My maternal grandfather, Frederick Stephen Keen (1874-
1949), and his wife, Gertrude Lucy Hall Keen (c.1883-1967), lived 
in a house on the west side of the Lamoille River traveling towards 
Greensboro Bend where the Route 16 bridge replaced the "back 
then" covered bridge adjacent to the house in which my mother 
and her siblings grew up. I believe the covered bridge was washed 
away during the flood of 1927. My mother loved her life there and 
always maintained her love for Vermont. She and my father left 
Vermont shortly after their 1935 marriage in Hardwick. Despite 
living outside Vermont1  for more than 65 years, they asked to be 
returned to Hardwick for internment in Fairview Cemetery.  My 
mother told us kids the following story. 
Her father, Fred Keen, made a bit of his own brew during pro-

He may also have sold some on the side. He also hid at least one 
bottle in his wife's bedroom dresser. 
One day there came a knock on the door. There stood a local 
constable of some variety, which my mother referred to as the lo-
cal sheriff. She said the officer was boisterous, threatening, and 
belligerent; it was believed there may have been a personal grudge 
against my grandfather that incited the incident. In any event, the 
bottle of privately made alcohol was found in my grandmother's 
dresser.
At that point, my grandfather confessed that it was both his 
product and his bottle, and he insisted that my grandmother knew 
nothing of it, since he had hidden the bottle in her dresser without 
telling her. The constable was having nothing of it--whether in-

What is a Fire District?1
The Vermont State Legislature first allowed town selectboards 
to create fire districts in the 1850s provided they received peti-
tions signed by 20 or more residents of the proposed district. The 
initial legislation intended fire districts to be served by a publicly 
owned and operated fire department. Over time the fire district be-
came the governmental structure used most commonly for special 
services in small communities within towns, especially water and 
sewer services.
In creating a fire district, a town's Selectboard establishes the 
district and defines its limits. In their application, the residents 
will have specified the powers they want the district to have.  Once 
created, the fire district is a corporate body which "operates like 
a town within a town." It holds an annual meeting and special 
meetings as necessary. It elects its own "prudential committee," 
and can even adopt a town manager form of governance, hav-
ing a manager direct day-to-day operations while the prudential 
committee makes policy decisions. A fire district can levy its own 
taxes, based on the town's Grand List, to pay for fire protection, 
water systems, including reservoirs and dams, sewage systems, 
sidewalks, public parks, street lighting, and "other lawful purpos-
es." It can also issue bonds. The prudential committee may make 
contracts and it may purchase equipment and real property. Fi-
nally, the fire district has the power of eminent domain. 
Elizabeth H. Dow

Historical Sketch of 
the East Hardwick Fire District
E. Brown Fay wrote the 
following pamphlet, published 
about 1944; this version has 
received some editing. Fay 
had served on the Prudential 
Committee of the East Hard-
wick Fire District since 1925. 
In November, 1912, the 
Selectmen of the Town of 
Hardwick, C.A. Stanford, T.G. 
Bronson and C.L. French, in 
response to a petition signed 
by more than 20 legal voters 
of the town, established the 
East Hardwick Fire District 
No. 1 (EHFD), and fixed the 
boundaries to encompass the 
entire Village of East Hard-
wick.1 In the organizational 
meeting, the fire district resi-
dents elected three men to a Prudential Committee of Trustees to 
manage the District.2
At a meeting held in May, 1913, the residents voted to buy 167 
shares of stock of the East Hardwick Water Supply System and 
Village Improve­ment Company, at $30.00 per share, or $5,010.00; 
they also voted to instruct the Prudential Committee to hire3 funds 
for current expenses and to ex­tend [the] water system. They stipu-
lated that the hired amount should not exceed $500.00.
On February 20, 1914, the residents again instructed the Pru-
dential Committee to buy the same 167 shares of stock at  $31.00 
per share, or $5,177.00. Noth­ing seems to have come from either 
of these votes as there is no further mention of them in the re-
cords.
The first fire district tax, passed in 1917 at $.20 on a dollar, 
paid for street lights and other necessary expenses of the village.4
At a Fire District meeting on October 31, 1923, the fire district 
residents voted to purchase the property of the East Hardwick 
A Pratt and Cady hydrant in  
East Hardwick.

12
Water Supply System and Village Im­provement Company, and to 
issue 70 bonds of $100.00 each, at no more than 5%, to pay for 
same. The bonds matured serially and cost a total of $3,590.00, 
making the cost of the district's water system a total of $10,590.00. 
But in our water system we have good value for our investment.
The reservoir was materially enlarged in 1942, so that it is 90 
by 110 feet with an average depth of six feet. The water is supplied 
chiefly by six large springs, with many smaller springs contribut-
ing also.
The water is brought to the village through an eight inch pipe 
for half the distance and six inch pipe the remainder. The main 
lines in the village are all four inch. In 1934 the line was extended 
past the new school building5 to a point on the Greensboro Bend 
road in front of the house now occupied by James Nicholson,6 and 
two years ago7 we put in an extension of 750 feet on Church Street 
to the Vermont Dairies, Inc., plant8 and set another hydrant, mak-
ing eight hydrants in all.
In addition to the property connected with the water system 
the Village owns the small lot, formerly occupied by the Arthur 
Montgomery store,9 at the westerly end of the bridge.This lot will 
be graded and will provide a small parking space and will no lon-
ger be used as a public dump.
The Fire District also owns the artesian well on the old Lam-
oille Valley Creamery Company's lot,10 together with a strip of land 
18 by 75 feet giving access to the highway.
The fire district now supplies 50 families, (150 persons), two 
stores, two filling stations, the school building, the Freeze Locker 
plant,11 the plant of the Vermont Dairies, Inc., which uses a 2 
inch pipe carrying thousands of gallons of water daily, and three 
farms.
Early in the year Trustees, E. B. Fay, F. D. Eldridge and C. H. 
Olmstead, decided to make a determined effort to collect all delin-
quent taxes and water rents.   What they expected to be a rather 
disagreeable task turned out to be a pleasant one because of the 
fine spirit of co­operation on the part of practically every one of the 
customers. By 1943, they had collected over $2000 and carried a 
balance of $569 with only $125 in arrears.
In 1925 the Fire District hired money to build a cement dam 
for their reservoir and to make repairs on the existing line across 
the the Lamoille River which had twice washed out. In 1943, the

Fire District still owed $2,730.84.
